{"self_assessment": "Impact: I proposed the fish early because its outline reads clearly, and the table committed to it. The body and nose are connected to the start, and so are both tail fin edges, so the judge should see a recognizable fish. The result is not clean, though. By my read about 131 of the 189 standing dominoes were connected to the start. The back edge of the tail is patchy, with pale pieces that are not joined to the run, and the bottom corner of the tail stayed rough. Those loose pieces may fall short or add noise to the tail. I'd call it a likely success, not a certain one.

Execution: I laid the top body run and it reached the tail on time. My own fix at the bottom corner of the tail did not take, and I should have inspected that joint earlier instead of discovering it late. Tom ended up laying the bottom body line, and I had said my hands were on both lines when they were not, which was inaccurate. I also left a stray line inside the body near the nose for a long time. It is harmless if it doesn't fall, but it was avoidable mess.

Collaboration: I used Priya's sketch instead of redrawing it, deferred to Tom when he said the bottom fin was already done, and kept clear of the corner while Tom and Maya worked there. Our status updates to the manager were mostly accurate. Because several of us were working near the tail, I could have coordinated the back-edge work better to avoid overlap.

Leadership: I set the animal and the initial split of work, then kept the table organized around strokes and joints. Once Priya and Tom stepped up, I gave them room instead of insisting on my plan. In the last two minutes I called a clean hands-off, which protected what was standing. My weak point was that my early assignments didn't match what people actually ended up doing, and I corrected them reactively instead of checking in sooner."}
